nN.description: Total number of nodes in the supply network (suppliers, transshipment points, and beneficiary camps)

node_type.description: Type of each node: $0$ = supplier, $1$ = transshipment point, $2$ = beneficiary camp

E.description: Adjacency matrix indicating whether a directed edge exists between each pair of nodes

dem.description: Number of beneficiaries at each beneficiary camp, in increasing order of node index

cap.description: Throughput capacity, in kg, of each transshipment point, in increasing order of node index

pc.description: Procurement cost per kg of each commodity

tc.description: Transportation cost per kg of each commodity along each edge

nutreq.description: Per-person nutritional requirement for each nutrient

nutval.description: Nutritional value per kg of each commodity for each nutrient

notes: We add implicit assumptions that all sets are non-empty and $\mathrm{dem}_j, \mathrm{cap}_t, \mathrm{pc}_k, \mathrm{tc}_{ijk}, \mathrm{nutreq}_\ell, \mathrm{nutval}_{k\ell} \geq 0$.
We assume the directed supply graph has no arcs entering suppliers and no arcs leaving beneficiary camps.

{cite:t}`ferchtandiker2025` state that transshipment points have limited capacity but do not model it, and let shipments be continuous. We add the throughput capacities $\mathrm{cap}_t$, shared across commodities, and require shipments to be whole numbers of kg.

The problem is NP-hard: shipments are integral and the transshipment capacities couple the commodities, so the problem contains integral multi-commodity flow, which is NP-hard even for two commodities {cite:t}`even1976`.
